title: The sock cymbal and learning to play with both feet
summary: Before the sock cymbal he used one foot; Abner Jones's bought pair of cymbals on sticks taught him to keep time with both feet.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: Well, so all the drum that you had at home was still the drum that your mother bought you?
Right.
Because we talked about you playing in the pit band, and said they didn't know you'd be practicing at home.
Well, I just only practiced with the little drum that I had.
Yeah.
And I had no bass drum. I could keep time with my foot, anyway.
Right.
And that was during the time just before the sock cymbal came out.
Oh, really?
And when it came out, it was like a low boy, plop cymbal.
Oh, really? There were different names for it.
Did it?
Right.
That's what Jo Jones was so terrific with, wasn't it?
Right, right. That's right.
But not everybody was using it then.
Well, they would set like two pieces of stick with a spring on it, and he would go flat down, you know what I mean.
Yeah.
And they started using it. Abner Jones, he had one that he bought, which was two pieces of stick with two cymbals on it, he'd keep offbeat with it.
Yeah. So did you get a chance to use it then, right there?
That's the way I learned. That's the way I learned to -- both feet.
I see. Yeah, that was lucky then, wasn't it? Because before that, you didn't use both feet.
No, just only one, see.
Yeah.
And, like, with --
So drummers really didn't get to use two feet until the sock cymbal came in, then.
Right.
Is that right?
But with the Mack David --
Yeah.
See, I didn't have no sock cymbal then.
No.
I didn't have that. I was just only using the bass drum.
